title: 1. What is JavaScript?
theory:
JavaScript (JS) is a lightweight, interpreted, object-oriented language with first-class functions. Originally built for web browsers (Netscape, 1995), it is now used everywhere (Node.js, Mobile, Desktop).

Key characteristics:
1. Dynamically typed
2. Single-threaded (but supports asynchronous operations via Event Loop)
3. Prototype-based object orientation.

title: 2. JS Engine & V8
output:
[V8 Architecture]
Source Code -> Parser -> AST -> Ignition Interpreter -> Bytecode -> TurboFan -> Machine Code
theory:
JS cannot run directly on the CPU. It needs an Engine. Chrome uses 'V8', Firefox uses 'SpiderMonkey'.
V8 compiles JS directly into native machine code before executing it, using JIT (Just-In-Time) compilation. This makes modern JS incredibly fast.

title: 3. Execution Context
output:
Memory Creation Phase...
Code Execution Phase...
theory:
Everything in JS happens inside an Execution Context. It has two components:
1. Memory Component (Variable Environment): Where variables & functions are stored as key-value pairs.
2. Code Component (Thread of Execution): Where code is executed one line at a time.

title: 4. Variables: var vs let vs const
theory: 'var' is function-scoped and can be redeclared. 'let' and 'const' are block-scoped (ES6). 'let' can be reassigned, but 'const' cannot be reassigned once initialized.

title: 5. Hoisting
theory: Hoisting is JS's default behavior of moving declarations to the top of the current scope. Variables declared with 'var' are hoisted and initialized with 'undefined'. 'let' and 'const' are also hoisted but remain in a 'Temporal Dead Zone' (TDZ).

title: 6. Data Types (Primitives)
theory:
Primitive types store a single value and are immutable. The memory is stored on the Stack.
Types: String, Number, BigInt, Boolean, Undefined, Null, Symbol.
code:
let name = 'Alice'; // String
let age = 21; // Number
let isStudent = true; // Boolean
let marks; // Undefined
let missing = null; // Null (Object bug)

console.log(typeof age); // 'number'

title: 7. Data Types (Non-Primitives)
theory:
Non-primitives (Reference Types) are mutable and stored in the Heap memory. Variables on the stack store a reference (memory address) to the heap location.
Types: Object, Array, Function.

title: 8. Stack vs Heap Memory
theory:
Stack memory is fast and holds primitive values and references. Heap memory is slower, large, and holds objects/arrays.
When you assign a primitive, it copies the value. When you assign an object, it copies the reference.

title: 9. Type Conversion & Coercion
theory:
Conversion is explicit (manual). Coercion is implicit (automatic by JS).
JS automatically converts types during loose equality (==) or arithmetic, which can lead to weird results.

title: 10. Arithmetic Operators
theory: Operators manipulate values. Arithmetic operators include +, -, *, /, % (modulo), ** (exponentiation), ++ (increment), -- (decrement).
code:
let a = 10, b = 5;
console.log(a + b); // 15
console.log(10 % 3); // 1 (Remainder)
console.log(2 ** 3); // 8 (2^3)

let count = 0;
count++; // count is 1
--count; // count is 0

title: 11. Comparison & Logical
theory:
Comparison: == (loose equality), === (strict equality - checks type too), !=, !==, >, <, >=, <=.
Logical: && (AND), || (OR), ! (NOT).

title: 12. Control Flow: if/else
theory: Conditional statements control execution flow based on boolean expressions. JS evaluates the expression in the parenthesis to true or false (truthy or falsy).

title: 13. Truthy and Falsy Values
theory:
In JS, every value has an inherent boolean value. 
Falsy values: false, 0, '', null, undefined, NaN.
Everything else is Truthy (e.g., 'hello', 42, [], {}).

title: 14. Ternary Operator
theory:
A shorthand for if/else. Syntax: 
condition ? expressionIfTrue : expressionIfFalse.
Great for assigning variables based on a condition in a single line.

title: 15. Switch Statement
theory: Used to perform different actions based on different strict equality (===) checks. Use 'break' to prevent fall-through (executing the next cases accidentally).

title: 16. Loops: For Loop
theory:
Loops execute a block of code repeatedly. The 'for' loop is used when you know exactly how many times you want to loop. 
Syntax: for (initialization; condition; increment)

title: 17. While and Do-While
output:
> Count: 0
> Count: 1
> Will run at least once!
theory:
While: Evaluates condition before executing. May never run.
Do-While: Evaluates condition after executing block. GUARANTEED to run at least once.

title: 18. Break and Continue
theory:
Break: Exits the loop entirely immediately.
Continue: Skips the current iteration and jumps to the next iteration of the loop.

title: 19. Functions: Declarations
theory: A function is a block of code designed to perform a particular task. Function declarations are hoisted, meaning they can be called before they are defined in the code.

title: 20. Function Expressions
theory: A function expression is when you store a function inside a variable. These are NOT hoisted. You must define them before calling them.

title: 21. Arrow Functions (ES6)
theory: Introduced in ES6, they provide a shorter syntax. If the function has one statement, you can omit the {} and 'return' keyword. Arrow functions also do not bind their own 'this'.

title: 22. Scope Chain & Lexical Environment
theory: Lexical Environment = Local Memory + Lexical Env of its Parent. When a variable isn't found locally, JS engines look up the Scope Chain to the parent, then grandparent, up to Global scope.

title: 23. Closures (Very Important!)
theory: A closure is a function bundled together with its lexical environment. A function 'remembers' the variables of its outer scope even after the outer function has finished executing!

title: 24. IIFE
theory: Immediately Invoked Function Expression. It runs as soon as it is defined. Great for data privacy and avoiding polluting the global namespace.

title: 25. Arrays & Accessing
theory: Arrays are special objects used to store ordered collections. They can hold mixed data types. Indexed from 0.
